**PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT**

**This document was prepared by Ashworth, Bledsoe & Cahill LLP at the direction of counsel for Redstone Capital Partners Fund IV, LP in connection with the proposed acquisition of Heartland Industrial Supply, Inc. This document constitutes attorney work product and is protected from disclosure by the attorney-client privilege, the work product doctrine, and all other applicable privileges. Distribution of this document is strictly limited to authorized recipients of Redstone Capital Partners Fund IV, LP and its advisors. Any unauthorized review, use, disclosure, or distribution is prohibited.**

**[CONFIDENTIAL --- TAX DUE DILIGENCE REPORT]{.underline}**

**[Heartland Industrial Supply, Inc.]{.underline}**

**(EIN: 38-3291045)**

Prepared by:

**Ashworth, Bledsoe & Cahill LLP** 200 S. Wacker Drive, Suite 3100 Chicago, Illinois 60606

**Victoria Chen**, Tax Partner **Ryan Kowalski**, Senior Associate

Engagement Partner: **Marcus Halpern**

Prepared for:

**Redstone Capital Partners Fund IV, LP** (EIN: 88-4521937)

**Redstone Capital GP IV, LLC** (EIN: 88-4521940)

**November 18, 2024**

**PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT** *Do not distribute without authorization*

Right-click to update Table of Contents

**[I. Executive Summary]{.underline}**

**[A. Engagement Scope]{.underline}**

Ashworth, Bledsoe & Cahill LLP (\"ABC\" or the \"Firm\") was retained by Redstone Capital Partners Fund IV, LP (\"Fund IV\"), a Delaware limited partnership, in connection with Fund IV\'s proposed acquisition of one hundred percent (100%) of the outstanding equity interests of Heartland Industrial Supply, Inc. (\"HIS\" or the \"Target\"), a Michigan S-corporation (EIN: 38-3291045; Michigan Corporate ID: 80-142-937). The proposed transaction contemplates an enterprise value of \$385,000,000 and an equity value of \$344,500,000 (calculated as the \$385,000,000 enterprise value less \$47,300,000 of net debt plus \$6,800,000 of balance sheet cash). The closing of the transaction is expected to occur on or about January 31, 2025.

The Target is a specialty industrial distribution business headquartered at 4700 Industrial Parkway, Grand Rapids, Michigan 49512. HIS employs 342 individuals, operates eight regional distribution centers, and conducts business across fourteen states. The Target\'s ownership consists of four members of the Kressler family, each of whom is a United States citizen and a resident of the State of Michigan.

**[B. Summary of Key Findings]{.underline}**

Our tax due diligence review has identified the following key findings, each of which is discussed in greater detail in the body of this report:

1\. **S-Corporation Status Confirmed.** HIS has maintained valid and continuous S-corporation status under Section 1362 of the Internal Revenue Code since January 1, 2001 --- a period of approximately twenty-three years. No events have been identified that would have caused an inadvertent or voluntary termination of the S-election during the review period.

2\. **Section 1374 Built-In Gains Tax --- Not Applicable.** HIS converted from C-corporation to S-corporation status effective January 1, 2001. The Section 1374 recognition period (permanently set at five years under the PATH Act of 2015 for elections made prior to 2012) expired on December 31, 2005. No corporate-level built-in gains tax will apply to the proposed transaction.

3\. **LIFO Recapture Exposure.** HIS uses the LIFO inventory method and maintains a LIFO reserve of approximately \$11,800,000. Under Section 1363(d), termination of the S-election --- which is effectively unavoidable in connection with any structure for this transaction --- will trigger a corporate-level LIFO recapture tax estimated at \$2,478,000 (federal) plus applicable state-level taxes. The allocation of this tax cost between buyer and sellers must be negotiated and addressed in the definitive purchase agreement.

4\. **Aggregate Shareholder Stock Basis.** The aggregate adjusted tax basis of the four Kressler shareholders in their HIS stock is approximately \$16,400,000.

5\. **Aggregate Inside Asset Basis and Step-Up Opportunity.** The aggregate adjusted tax basis of all HIS assets is approximately \$134,200,000, creating a potential basis step-up of \$250,800,000 if a structure yielding a stepped-up basis (such as a Section 338(h)(10) election) is employed.

6\. **Multi-State Filing and State Conformity Issues.** HIS files income and franchise tax returns in fourteen states. Not all states conform to the federal Section 338(h)(10) election, with Pennsylvania specifically identified as a non-conforming jurisdiction. State conformity directly affects the buyer\'s ability to claim a stepped-up basis and the sellers\' gain characterization at the state level.

7\. **Rollover Equity.** David Kressler intends to roll \$12,000,000 of equity into the post-closing acquisition structure. The interaction between the rollover and any Section 338(h)(10) election, as well as the choice of acquisition vehicle entity classification, creates significant structural questions requiring resolution.

**[C. Structural Considerations]{.underline}**

The choice of transaction structure --- a straight stock purchase, a stock purchase with a Section 338(h)(10) election, or a direct asset purchase --- has significant tax implications for both the buyer and the selling shareholders. This report identifies the relevant structural considerations and open questions. A separate tax structure memorandum will be prepared to quantify the economic impact of each alternative and recommend an optimal structure.

**[D. Scope of Review]{.underline}**

In connection with this engagement, we reviewed the following materials and conducted the following diligence activities: HIS federal income tax returns (Forms 1120-S) and Schedules K-1 for tax years 2019 through 2023; the original Form 2553 (S-Corporation Election) and IRS acknowledgment letter; shareholder basis schedules and distribution records; asset depreciation schedules and fixed asset registers; inventory records and LIFO reserve computation workpapers; state income and franchise tax returns for all fourteen filing jurisdictions (2019--2023); employment tax records (Forms 941, W-2 summaries) for 2022 and 2023; property tax filings; and sales and use tax returns (sample returns for 2022--2023). We conducted interviews with Dale Forsberg, Managing Partner, Ridgeline Accounting Group, 840 Monroe Center Street, Grand Rapids, Michigan 49503 (HIS\'s outside accounting firm), and with the Kressler family shareholders. We reviewed documents made available through the electronic data room and coordinated with Prescott & Lowell LLP (seller\'s counsel; 125 Ottawa Avenue NW, Suite 800, Grand Rapids, Michigan 49503; lead partner Theresa Bridgman) and Summit Ridge Advisors (sell-side investment bank; Managing Director Kevin Tanaka).

**[II. S-Corporation Status Confirmation]{.underline}**

**[II.A. History of Entity Formation and S-Election]{.underline}**

Heartland Industrial Supply, Inc. was incorporated in the State of Michigan in 1997 by Gerald Kressler. From the date of its incorporation through December 31, 2000, HIS operated as a Subchapter C corporation for federal income tax purposes. During these C-corporation years, HIS generated taxable income and accumulated earnings and profits (\"E&P\") in the ordinary course of its operations.

Effective January 1, 2001, HIS filed IRS Form 2553, Election by a Small Business Corporation, to elect S-corporation status under Section 1362(a) of the Internal Revenue Code. We reviewed a copy of the executed Form 2553, which bears the signatures of all shareholders who held stock as of the date of the election. The Internal Revenue Service acknowledged and accepted the S-election by determination letter dated March 14, 2001.

At the time of the S-election, HIS had accumulated E&P from the C-corporation years (1997--2000). We have confirmed through a review of distribution records and discussions with Dale Forsberg of Ridgeline Accounting Group that all pre-2001 accumulated E&P was distributed to the shareholders prior to the S-election becoming effective. As a result, as of the date of this report, HIS has no accumulated E&P from its C-corporation years. This finding eliminates any concerns regarding the application of the Section 1368 ordering rules, which could otherwise cause distributions from an S-corporation with accumulated C-corporation E&P to be characterized as dividends (taxable at ordinary income rates to the extent of accumulated E&P) rather than returns of capital or capital gain.

Since the effective date of the S-election on January 1, 2001, HIS has maintained continuous, unbroken S-corporation status through the present date --- a period of approximately twenty-three years. We have identified no events during this period that would have caused an inadvertent or voluntary termination of the S-election, including no disqualifying transfers of stock to ineligible shareholders, no issuance of a second class of stock, and no period in which the number of shareholders exceeded one hundred.

**[II.B. Eligible Shareholder Analysis]{.underline}**

Section 1361(b)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code limits S-corporation shareholders to individuals (who are citizens or residents of the United States), certain trusts described in Section 1361(c)(2), and estates, with a maximum of one hundred shareholders. As of the date of this report, the current shareholders of HIS, their respective ownership percentages, and their eligibility status are as follows:

  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Shareholder**      **Ownership**   **Citizenship**   **Residency**   **Eligible**
  -------------------- --------------- ----------------- --------------- --------------
  Gerald Kressler      62%             U.S. Citizen      Michigan        Yes

  Patricia Kressler    18%             U.S. Citizen      Michigan        Yes

  David Kressler       10%             U.S. Citizen      Michigan        Yes

  Sarah Kressler-Cho   10%             U.S. Citizen      Michigan        Yes
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

All four shareholders are individuals who are citizens of the United States and residents of the State of Michigan. No shareholder is a nonresident alien. No shares of HIS stock are held by or for the benefit of any trust, estate, partnership, corporation, or other entity. At no time during the review period has any HIS stock been held by an ineligible shareholder.

HIS has only one class of stock outstanding --- common stock. HIS has never issued any convertible instruments, preferred stock, warrants, options, or any other instruments that could constitute a second class of stock within the meaning of Section 1361(b)(1)(D) and Treasury Regulation § 1.1361-1(l). We have confirmed that there is no outstanding corporate-level debt owed by HIS to any shareholder that could be recharacterized as equity under the economic substance or debt-equity principles. Furthermore, there are no disproportionate distribution rights among the shareholders --- all distributions have been made strictly in accordance with the shareholders\' pro-rata stock ownership percentages.

**Conclusion.** No issues have been identified that would jeopardize the validity of HIS\'s S-corporation election for any open tax year or for the period preceding the proposed transaction closing date.

**[II.C. Section 1374 Built-In Gains Tax Analysis]{.underline}**

Because HIS converted from C-corporation to S-corporation status on January 1, 2001, it was potentially subject to the built-in gains (\"BIG\") tax under Section 1374 of the Internal Revenue Code during the recognition period following the conversion. The Section 1374 BIG tax is a corporate-level tax imposed on an S-corporation\'s recognized built-in gains during the applicable recognition period, at the highest corporate tax rate.

At the time of the S-election (January 1, 2001), HIS had a net unrealized built-in gain (\"NUBIG\") of approximately \$14,700,000, comprising the following components:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Component**                       **Amount**
  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Real property appreciation          \$6,200,000

  Equipment appreciation              \$3,100,000

  LIFO reserve recapture              \$5,400,000

  **Total NUBIG**                     **\$14,700,000**
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

**However, the Section 1374 recognition period has expired.** Under the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015, the recognition period for S-elections made prior to 2012 was permanently set at five years. For HIS, which elected S-corporation status effective January 1, 2001, the recognition period ended on December 31, 2005 --- nearly nineteen years before the proposed closing date of January 31, 2025. Accordingly, any gains recognized in connection with the proposed transaction, whether through an actual asset sale, a deemed asset sale pursuant to a Section 338(h)(10) election, or any other disposition, will **not** be subject to the corporate-level BIG tax under Section 1374.

This conclusion applies regardless of the transaction structure ultimately selected. Whether the parties pursue a straight stock sale, a stock sale with a Section 338(h)(10) election, or a direct asset sale, the expiration of the Section 1374 recognition period eliminates any exposure to this corporate-level tax.

**Important Distinction.** The expiration of the Section 1374 recognition period does **not** eliminate the potential LIFO recapture tax under Section 1363(d), which is a separate corporate-level tax provision that applies independently of the BIG recognition period. Section 1363(d) is triggered by the termination of an S-election --- not by the passage of a recognition period --- and remains fully applicable to the proposed transaction. The LIFO recapture exposure is discussed in detail in Section IV.B of this report.

**Conclusion.** Section 1374 built-in gains tax is **not** applicable to the proposed transaction. The \$14,700,000 historical NUBIG is no longer a tax exposure.

**[III. Shareholder Basis Analysis]{.underline}**

**[III.A. Methodology]{.underline}**

We reconstructed each shareholder\'s adjusted tax basis in their HIS stock by reviewing original capitalization documents, articles of incorporation and amendments, annual S-corporation K-1 schedules (Forms 1120-S, Schedule K-1) for tax years 2001 through 2023, shareholder distribution records maintained by HIS and Ridgeline Accounting Group, and shareholder loan documentation (of which there is none). We also reviewed 2024 interim financial statements and estimated 2024 K-1 amounts based on discussions with Dale Forsberg of Ridgeline Accounting Group, incorporating projected operating results through the expected closing date of January 31, 2025.

Stock basis computations under Section 1367 reflect: (i) each shareholder\'s original basis (or, in the case of gifted shares, the carry-over basis from the donor); (ii) increases for cumulative pass-through income, including each shareholder\'s pro-rata share of ordinary income and separately stated items; and (iii) decreases for cumulative distributions received and any pass-through losses or deductions.

No shareholder has made any loans to HIS at any time during the S-corporation period, so there is no separate debt basis to track under Section 1367(b)(2). Similarly, no shareholder has pledged assets or personally guaranteed HIS indebtedness in a manner that would create additional basis under applicable case law.

**[III.B. Gerald Kressler --- 62% Shareholder]{.underline}**

Gerald Kressler, age 67, is the founder, majority shareholder, and Chief Executive Officer of HIS. Gerald is a resident of the State of Michigan. He intends to fully exit the business at closing and will not have any continuing operational role.

Gerald\'s adjusted stock basis is computed as follows:

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Item**                                                     **Amount**
  ------------------------------------------------------------ -----------------------------------
  Original cash contribution at incorporation (1997)           \$500,000

  Cumulative S-corporation pass-through income (2001--2024E)   \$41,200,000

  Less: Cumulative distributions received (2001--2024E)        (\$33,300,000)

  **Adjusted Tax Basis (estimated at closing)**                **\$8,400,000**
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Gerald\'s pro-rata share of equity value is 62% × \$344,500,000 = \$213,590,000, all of which will be received in cash. In a straight stock sale (without a Section 338(h)(10) election), Gerald\'s capital gain would be \$213,590,000 -- \$8,400,000 = \$205,190,000, all of which would be treated as long-term capital gain (Gerald has held his HIS stock continuously since 1997, well in excess of the one-year holding period requirement).

**[III.C. Patricia Kressler --- 18% Shareholder]{.underline}**

Patricia Kressler, age 64, is an 18% shareholder and the Chief Financial Officer of HIS. Patricia is a resident of the State of Michigan. She intends to fully exit the business at closing.

Patricia\'s adjusted stock basis is computed as follows:

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Item**                                                     **Amount**
  ------------------------------------------------------------ -----------------------------------
  Original basis                                               \$200,000

  Cumulative S-corporation pass-through income (2001--2024E)   \$11,900,000

  Less: Cumulative distributions received (2001--2024E)        (\$8,300,000)

  **Adjusted Tax Basis (estimated at closing)**                **\$3,800,000**
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Patricia\'s pro-rata share of equity value is 18% × \$344,500,000 = \$62,010,000, all of which will be received in cash. In a straight stock sale, Patricia\'s capital gain would be \$62,010,000 -- \$3,800,000 = \$58,210,000, all long-term capital gain.

**[III.D. David Kressler --- 10% Shareholder]{.underline}**

David Kressler, age 38, is a 10% shareholder and the Vice President of Operations of HIS. David is a resident of the State of Michigan. David will remain with the company following the closing under a three-year employment agreement (through January 31, 2028) and will be subject to a five-year non-compete agreement (through January 31, 2030).

David\'s adjusted stock basis is computed as follows:

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Item**                                                                         **Amount**
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Original basis (acquired stock by gift from Gerald Kressler; carry-over basis)   \$100,000

  Cumulative S-corporation pass-through income (2001--2024E)                       \$6,600,000

  Less: Cumulative distributions received (2001--2024E)                            (\$4,600,000)

  **Adjusted Tax Basis (estimated at closing)**                                    **\$2,100,000**
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

David\'s pro-rata share of equity value is 10% × \$344,500,000 = \$34,450,000, of which \$12,000,000 will be rollover equity and \$22,450,000 will be cash (\$22,450,000 + \$12,000,000 = \$34,450,000). In a straight stock sale, David\'s capital gain would be \$34,450,000 -- \$2,100,000 = \$32,350,000, all long-term capital gain (David received the stock by gift and tacks Gerald\'s holding period under Section 1223(2), which extends back to 1997).

**Rollover Equity Note.** David\'s \$12,000,000 equity rollover into the post-closing acquisition structure raises significant structural questions. If a Section 338(h)(10) election is made, David\'s HIS stock is deemed sold in its entirety, and his rollover would need to be structured as a separate transaction (e.g., as a contribution to the acquisition partnership under Section 721, or as a Section 351 contribution if a corporate acquisition vehicle is used) to achieve tax deferral on the rollover portion. The interaction between the 338(h)(10) election and the rollover must be carefully analyzed. **This issue is flagged for the tax structure memorandum.** See Section VIII.B below.

**[III.E. Sarah Kressler-Cho --- 10% Shareholder]{.underline}**

Sarah Kressler-Cho, age 35, is a 10% shareholder. Sarah is a resident of the State of Michigan and is not involved in the day-to-day operations of HIS. She will fully exit at closing and receive her entire share of equity value in cash.

**[IV.B. LIFO Inventory Method and Recapture Exposure]{.underline}**

HIS has used the LIFO (last-in, first-out) inventory method for both tax and financial reporting purposes since at least 2001. The LIFO conformity requirement under Section 472(c) mandates that a taxpayer using LIFO for tax purposes must also use LIFO for financial reporting purposes, and HIS has complied with this requirement throughout the review period. The LIFO reserve as of December 31, 2024 (estimated, based on discussions with Ridgeline Accounting Group) is **\$11,800,000**. The LIFO inventory basis is \$64,200,000, while the FIFO-equivalent inventory value is \$76,000,000.

**LIFO Recapture Risk under Section 1363(d).** If HIS\'s S-corporation election terminates --- whether by voluntary revocation under Section 1362(d)(1), a disqualifying event under Section 1362(d)(2), or a deemed termination in connection with a Section 338(h)(10) election --- Section 1363(d) requires the corporation to include the LIFO recapture amount (i.e., the excess of the FIFO value of inventory over the LIFO value, which is the \$11,800,000 LIFO reserve) in gross income in the corporation\'s last S-corporation tax year. Unlike most S-corporation income, which passes through to the shareholders, the resulting tax on this LIFO recapture amount is paid at the **corporate level** at the applicable corporate income tax rate (currently 21% federal), not by the shareholders individually.

Estimated federal corporate-level LIFO recapture tax: \$11,800,000 × 21% = **\$2,478,000**. Additional state-level LIFO recapture taxes may apply depending on state treatment. For example, Michigan may impose the 6% Corporate Income Tax on the Michigan-apportioned portion of the LIFO recapture amount (see Section V.C below). Other states in HIS\'s filing footprint may similarly impose state-level corporate taxes on the LIFO recapture income. This corporate-level tax directly reduces the net proceeds available to the selling shareholders.

**[V.B. State Conformity to Section 338(h)(10) --- Key Concern]{.underline}**

**This is a critical issue for the tax structure memorandum.** Not all states in HIS\'s filing footprint conform to the federal Section 338(h)(10) election. If a Section 338(h)(10) election is made at the federal level, certain states may not recognize the deemed asset sale, instead treating the transaction as a stock sale for state income tax purposes. This non-conformity would result in: (i) no stepped-up basis in assets for state tax purposes in those non-conforming states, thereby reducing the buyer\'s state-level amortization and depreciation deductions; and (ii) potentially different gain characterization for sellers at the state level, which could create discrepancies between federal and state tax reporting positions.

**Preliminary Findings on State Conformity:**

**Pennsylvania.** Pennsylvania does not follow IRC Section 338(h)(10) for Corporate Net Income Tax (CNIT) purposes. The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue has consistently taken the position that a federal 338(h)(10) election does not alter the character of the transaction for Pennsylvania tax purposes, and the transaction would be treated as a stock sale for Pennsylvania CNIT. As a result, the buyer would not receive a stepped-up basis in HIS\'s assets for purposes of computing Pennsylvania-apportioned taxable income. Pennsylvania accounts for approximately 6% of HIS\'s apportionment, which is a meaningful but not dominant share of the overall tax base.

**Other States.** Most other states in HIS\'s filing footprint generally conform to the federal treatment of a Section 338(h)(10) election, but specific conformity should be confirmed for each jurisdiction through a detailed state-by-state analysis. In particular, conformity should be verified for Tennessee (which has a unique excise tax structure), Kentucky (given the LLET), and Ohio (though the CAT is a gross receipts tax and the 338(h)(10) election is not directly relevant to Ohio\'s commercial activity tax computation).

**Seller Impact.** In non-conforming states, the sellers may still be subject to state income tax on their gain under the state\'s characterization of the transaction as a stock sale, which could differ from the federal characterization as a deemed asset sale. This creates the potential for inconsistent treatment across jurisdictions and, in certain scenarios, a risk of economic double taxation at the state level, where the same gain is effectively taxed to both the seller (as stock sale gain) and subsequently to the buyer (as income earned on assets with an unreduced basis).

**Recommendation.** The tax structure memorandum should include a detailed state-by-state conformity analysis for all fourteen filing jurisdictions and quantify the economic impact of non-conformity on both buyer and sellers. The results of this analysis may influence the choice of transaction structure and the allocation of tax costs in the definitive purchase agreement.

**[V.C. Michigan-Specific Tax Considerations]{.underline}**

Michigan is HIS\'s domicile state and largest apportionment jurisdiction, representing 28% of the total apportionment factor. The following Michigan-specific tax considerations are relevant to the proposed transaction:

**Michigan Corporate Income Tax (CIT).** Michigan imposes the CIT at a rate of 6% on the taxable income of C-corporations apportioned to Michigan. S-corporations are not subject to the CIT; instead, income passes through to shareholders who pay Michigan individual income tax at 4.25% on their respective shares of distributive income. If HIS converts to a C-corporation (or if the S-election terminates as a result of the transaction), the post-closing entity would become subject to the 6% CIT on Michigan-apportioned income. This represents an incremental entity-level tax cost of 1.75% (6% CIT minus 4.25% individual rate) on Michigan income, before considering the deductibility of state taxes at the federal level.

**Michigan Individual Income Tax.** All four Kressler shareholders are Michigan residents. Michigan imposes a flat 4.25% income tax on all taxable income, including capital gains. Michigan does not provide a preferential rate for long-term capital gains. Accordingly, the Kressler shareholders\' gain on the sale of their HIS stock --- regardless of whether the gain is long-term capital gain or ordinary income at the federal level --- will be subject to Michigan income tax at the uniform 4.25% rate.

**Pass-Through Entity Withholding.** Under the Michigan Income Tax Act, S-corporations with nonresident shareholders are required to withhold Michigan income tax on the nonresident\'s share of distributive income. Since all four HIS shareholders are Michigan residents, this withholding requirement is not applicable to the proposed transaction. However, if HIS has any nonresident employees with equity participation interests (stock options, phantom equity units, or similar arrangements), a composite return filing obligation may arise. Based on our review of corporate records and discussions with management, we have not identified any equity participation plans for non-shareholder employees, but this should be confirmed with management and Ridgeline Accounting Group prior to closing.

**Michigan LIFO Recapture.** To the extent LIFO recapture tax is imposed at the corporate level under Section 1363(d), Michigan may impose the 6% CIT on the Michigan-apportioned portion of the LIFO recapture amount. Estimated Michigan LIFO recapture tax: \$11,800,000 × 28% (Michigan apportionment factor) × 6% (CIT rate) = approximately **\$198,240**. This amount is in addition to the \$2,478,000 federal LIFO recapture tax.

**[VIII. Structural Considerations]{.underline}**

*Note: This section identifies structural questions and alternatives for the proposed acquisition. These issues are flagged for detailed analysis in a separate tax structure memorandum to be prepared by the tax team. The observations and questions set forth below are preliminary in nature and do not constitute recommendations. The tax structure memorandum will provide quantitative analysis and a recommended course of action.*

**[VIII.A. Three Structural Alternatives]{.underline}**

The proposed transaction, as described in the signed Letter of Intent dated September 15, 2024, contemplates a purchase of 100% of the outstanding stock of HIS. The LOI provides that the parties will negotiate in good faith regarding a potential Section 338(h)(10) election and will cooperate on the purchase price allocation. Three principal structural alternatives should be analyzed in the tax structure memorandum:

**1. Straight Stock Purchase (No Election).** Under this alternative, Fund IV would purchase 100% of HIS stock from the four Kressler shareholders for the agreed equity value of \$344,500,000. HIS would continue as a separate legal entity with its existing tax attributes, including its historical aggregate asset basis of \$134,200,000. No step-up in the basis of HIS\'s assets would occur at the corporate level. The sellers would recognize gain equal to the difference between their respective stock sale proceeds and their respective stock bases. Aggregate stock sale gain would be \$328,100,000, all of which would be long-term capital gain. The primary disadvantage of this structure from the buyer\'s perspective is the lack of any stepped-up basis in the Target\'s assets, which means the buyer forfeits the present value of the tax benefit from amortizing and depreciating a \$250,800,000 basis step-up.

**2. Stock Purchase with Section 338(h)(10) Election.** Under this alternative, Fund IV would purchase 100% of HIS stock, and the buyer and the sellers would jointly make a Section 338(h)(10) election under Treasury Regulation § 1.338(h)(10)-1(c). For purposes of federal income tax, HIS would be treated as having sold all of its assets in a single deemed transaction on the acquisition date at fair market value, followed by a deemed distribution of the sale proceeds to the shareholders in complete liquidation of HIS. The buyer would receive a stepped-up basis in all of HIS\'s assets equal to the \"adjusted grossed-up basis\" (AGUB), as computed under Treasury Regulation § 1.338-5 and allocated among the assets under Section 1060 using the residual method. The gain on the deemed asset sale would flow through to the S-corporation shareholders on their final Schedules K-1. Gain character under this alternative would be mixed: ordinary income on Section 1245 recapture items

Direct Asset Purchase.** Under this alternative, HIS would sell all of its assets directly to the buyer (or a newly formed acquisition entity), followed by a liquidation of HIS and a distribution of the net sale proceeds to the Kressler shareholders. This alternative produces substantially the same federal income tax results as a Section 338(h)(10) election --- the buyer receives a stepped-up basis, and the sellers recognize gain on the deemed asset sale. However, a direct asset purchase introduces additional legal and practical complexity, including the necessity of transferring each individual asset (contracts, permits, licenses, real property deeds, equipment titles), obtaining third-party consents for assignment of contracts and leases, and the potential imposition of sales and use tax on the transfer of tangible personal property (equipment, inventory) in certain states. Additionally, any change-of-control provisions in HIS\'s customer or vendor agreements could be triggered differently in an asset purchase than in a stock purchase.
4	
5	**Preliminary Observation.** For an S-corporation target, the Section 338(h)(10) election typically offers the most favorable combination of: (i) legal simplicity (the stock transfer mechanism avoids the complexity of transferring individual assets); (ii) buyer benefit (the full stepped-up basis in all assets, including goodwill and intangibles); and (iii) acceptable seller tax treatment (gain flows through to the shareholders via the S-corporation pass-through mechanism, with most of the gain characterized as long-term capital gain). However, the LIFO recapture tax, the ordinary income characterization of certain gain components (Section 1245 recapture, inventory), and the state non-conformity issues identified in Section V.B create significant seller-side costs that must be quantified and compared to the stock sale alternative before a structural recommendation can be made.
6	
7	**Open Questions for Tax Structure Memorandum:**

9	> • What is the net present value of the buyer\'s tax benefit from the stepped-up basis (Section 197 amortization, equipment depreciation) under a 338(h)(10) election, using appropriate discount rates and the 2025 bonus depreciation percentage?
10	>
11	> • What is the incremental tax cost to the sellers of a 338(h)(10) election versus a straight stock sale, taking into account the mixed character of gain (ordinary income on recapture items and inventory, capital gain on real property and intangibles) and the corporate-level LIFO recapture tax?
12	>
13	> • How should the LIFO recapture tax of approximately \$2,478,000 (federal) plus state taxes be allocated between buyer and sellers in the definitive purchase agreement?
14	>
15	> • Does the aggregate buyer benefit from the step-up justify a \"gross-up\" or price adjustment to compensate the sellers for the incremental tax costs of a 338(h)(10) election?
16	>
17	> • How does David Kressler\'s \$12,000,000 rollover equity interact with the 338(h)(10) election, and can the rollover be structured to achieve tax deferral on the rolled-over portion?
18	>
19	> • What is the state-by-state impact of non-conforming jurisdictions (particularly Pennsylvania) on the buyer\'s stepped-up basis and the sellers\' gain characterization?

21	**[VIII.B. David Kressler Rollover Equity --- Structural Questions]{.underline}**
22	
23	David Kressler will roll \$12,000,000 of his equity proceeds into the post-closing acquisition structure. The buyer, Fund IV, is a Delaware limited partnership, and the acquisition vehicle will likely be structured as a pass-through entity (e.g., HIS Holdings, LLC). The following tax deferral options for the rollover should be analyzed in the tax structure memorandum:
24	
25	**Section 721 Contribution to Partnership.** If the acquisition vehicle is a partnership or a limited liability company taxed as a partnership for federal income tax purposes, David could contribute his rollover amount as a capital contribution under Section 721, which provides for non-recognition of gain or loss on a contribution of property to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest. However, under a 338(h)(10) election, David\'s HIS stock is deemed sold in its entirety (all ten percent), and he would first recognize gain on 100% of his HIS shares on the deemed asset sale. The rollover would then be structured as a functionally separate step: David receives cash for his full 10% interest in HIS and simultaneously (or promptly thereafter) contributes \$12,000,000 in cash to the acquisition partnership in exchange for a partnership interest. This is a two-step transaction, and the tax deferral on the rollover applies only to the second step (the partnership contribution), not to the first step (the deemed stock/asset sale).
26	
27	**Section 351 Contribution to Corporation.** Alternatively, if the acquisition vehicle is a corporation (or an LLC electing corporate treatment), David could contribute cash or property under Section 351 in exchange for stock, provided that the \"control\" requirement (80% ownership by the transferor or transferors) is satisfied immediately after the exchange. However, since Fund IV will own the vast majority of the acquisition entity (approximately 96.5%), David alone (holding approximately 3.5%) would not satisfy the 80% control threshold. Tax-free treatment under Section 351 would require that David be part of a \"control group\" that includes Fund IV\'s contribution, with all members of the group collectively owning 80% or more of the corporation immediately after the exchange.
28	
29	**Direct Stock-for-Interest Exchange.** A third possibility is structuring the rollover as a direct exchange of David\'s HIS stock (or a portion thereof) for interests in the acquisition entity, potentially qualifying for non-recognition under Section 721 (if the acquisition entity is a partnership) or Section 351 (if the acquisition entity is a corporation). However, this approach interacts complexly with the Section 338(h)(10) election, which deems all HIS stock as sold and does not naturally accommodate a partial non-recognition exchange of the target stock.
30

**CONFIDENTIAL**

**QUALITY OF EARNINGS REPORT**

**EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

\ 

**Heartland Industrial Supply, Inc.**

\ 

Prepared by:

**Ridgeline Accounting Group** 840 Monroe Center Street Grand Rapids, MI 49503

Managing Partner: Dale Forsberg, CPA

\ 

Prepared at the Request of:

**Redstone Capital Partners Fund IV, LP** (the \"Prospective Buyer\")

\ 

**Report Date: October 28, 2024**

\ 

*Engagement Period:* Financial analysis based on fiscal years ended December 31, 2021 through December 31, 2023, and interim period ended September 30, 2024, with management projections for the twelve months ended December 31, 2024 (\"2024E\").

\ 

**CONFIDENTIALITY NOTICE:** This report is confidential and has been prepared solely for the use of Redstone Capital Partners Fund IV, LP and its advisors, including Ashworth, Bledsoe & Cahill LLP and Summit Ridge Advisors. It may not be distributed to any other party without the prior written consent of Ridgeline Accounting Group.

**NOTE:** This executive summary should be read in conjunction with the full Quality of Earnings Report (Volumes I and II) and the accompanying data book.

**TABLE OF CONTENTS**

Right-click to update Table of Contents

**[I. Engagement Overview and Scope of Work]{.underline}**

Ridgeline Accounting Group (\"Ridgeline\" or \"we\") was engaged by Redstone Capital Partners Fund IV, LP (\"Fund IV\"), a Delaware limited partnership (EIN: 88-4521937), controlled by its general partner Redstone Capital GP IV, LLC (EIN: 88-4521940), to perform a quality of earnings analysis of Heartland Industrial Supply, Inc. (\"HIS\" or the \"Company\"), a Michigan S-corporation (EIN: 38-3291045; Michigan Corporate ID: 80-142-937).

HIS was incorporated in the State of Michigan in 1997. The Company elected S-corporation status effective January 1, 2001, pursuant to a timely filed Form 2553, and has maintained continuous S-corporation status since that date. As detailed further below, the Company\'s shareholder composition has at all times consisted exclusively of eligible S-corporation shareholders --- specifically, individual United States citizens who are Michigan residents.

The scope of our engagement includes the following principal areas of analysis:

> \(i\) analysis of the quality and sustainability of reported earnings;
>
> \(ii\) identification and assessment of EBITDA adjustments, including the nature, magnitude, and recurrence profile of each proposed adjustment;
>
> \(iii\) working capital analysis and establishment of a preliminary net working capital target for use in the purchase agreement;
>
> \(iv\) balance sheet review, with particular focus on asset valuation, inventory methodology, and the adequacy of reserves;
>
> \(v\) revenue quality and customer concentration review, including an assessment of the recurring nature of the Company\'s revenue streams; and
>
> \(vi\) assessment of accounting policies and their implications for a potential change-of-control transaction, including observations regarding the Company\'s S-corporation status, LIFO inventory methodology, and related tax considerations.

We note that Ridgeline has served as HIS\'s outside accountants since 2003 and has prepared all S-corporation tax returns (Form 1120-S and related state filings) for the Company during that period. We disclose this existing relationship in the interest of full transparency. Our quality of earnings work was performed by a separate engagement team, led by partners and staff with no involvement in the Company\'s recurring tax and accounting work, to maintain objectivity and independence.

In performing this engagement, we coordinated with the following parties and their advisors: Summit Ridge Advisors (sell-side investment bank; Managing Director: Kevin Tanaka), Prescott & Lowell LLP (seller\'s counsel; lead partner: Theresa Bridgman), and Pinnacle Valuation Services (engaged for purchase price allocation; principal: Amanda Reeves). We also provided requested information and access to Ashworth, Bledsoe & Cahill LLP (buyer\'s counsel; engagement partner: Marcus Halpern; tax partner: Victoria Chen; senior associate: Ryan Kowalski), who are advising Fund IV on all legal and tax aspects of the proposed transaction.

Our analysis is based on the following data sources: audited financial statements for fiscal years 2021 through 2023, unaudited interim financial statements for the nine months ended September 30, 2024, management-prepared 2024E budget and projections, general ledger data and subsidiary ledgers, federal and state tax returns for all periods under review, payroll records, lease agreements for all Company facilities, and extensive interviews with senior management, including Gerald Kressler (Chief Executive Officer and 62% shareholder), Patricia Kressler (Chief Financial Officer and 18% shareholder), and David Kressler (Vice President of Operations and 10% shareholder).

The proposed transaction contemplates an enterprise value of \$385,000,000. Based on the 2024E Adjusted EBITDA of \$41,850,000 (as discussed in Section IV below), this implies an EV/EBITDA multiple of approximately 9.2x. A Letter of Intent was signed by the parties on September 15, 2024. The expected date for signing of the definitive purchase agreement is December 6, 2024, with an anticipated closing date of January 31, 2025.

**[II. Company Overview]{.underline}**

Heartland Industrial Supply, Inc. is a specialty industrial distributor headquartered at 4700 Industrial Parkway, Grand Rapids, Michigan 49512. The Company was founded in 1997 by Gerald Kressler and initially operated as a C-corporation from its date of incorporation through December 31, 2000. Effective January 1, 2001, the Company elected S-corporation status pursuant to Section 1362(a) of the Internal Revenue Code, and it has maintained continuous S-corporation status without interruption since that date.

The Company\'s core business consists of the distribution of specialty industrial fasteners, gaskets, seals, and related engineered components to a broad base of manufacturing customers. HIS serves as a critical link in its customers\' supply chains, providing both standard catalogue items and custom-specified components essential to its customers\' manufacturing processes. The Company\'s product lines are consumable in nature --- fasteners, gaskets, and seals are used in production processes and require ongoing replenishment --- which provides the Company with a high degree of revenue visibility and recurring demand characteristics.

HIS maintains a geographic footprint spanning 14 states, anchored by its headquarters and primary distribution center, a 120,000-square-foot facility located in Grand Rapids, Michigan. The Company also operates eight regional distribution centers strategically positioned to serve its customer base across the Midwest, Southeast, and Mid-Atlantic regions. As of the date of this report, the Company employs 342 full-time employees across all locations.

The Company\'s outstanding shares of common stock are held by the following four shareholders, all of whom are Michigan residents and United States citizens:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Shareholder**                     **Ownership Percentage**
  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Gerald Kressler                     62%

  Patricia Kressler                   18%

  David Kressler                      10%

  Sarah Kressler-Cho                  10%

  **Total**                           **100%**
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

The Company has maintained a single class of common stock throughout the entirety of its existence as an S-corporation. There are no convertible instruments, no preferred stock, and no outstanding warrants or options that could create a second class of stock. There is no corporate-level debt owed to shareholders. All accumulated earnings and profits from the Company\'s C-corporation years (1997 through 2000) were distributed to shareholders prior to the effective date of the S-election, and accordingly, no accumulated earnings and profits from C-corporation years remain on the Company\'s books.

We note that the Company\'s S-corporation status is a key consideration for transaction structuring. Any change in entity status --- including potential termination of the S-election upon an acquisition by a non-eligible shareholder such as a limited partnership or corporation --- will have significant tax implications, including but not limited to LIFO recapture under Section 1363(d) of the Internal Revenue Code, which we discuss in detail in Section VI below. The parties\' respective tax advisors should carefully evaluate the consequences of S-election termination in the context of the proposed acquisition structure.

**[III. Revenue Quality Analysis]{.underline}**

**[III.A. Revenue Summary and Trends]{.underline}**

The Company\'s 2024E revenue is projected at \$412,800,000, reflecting steady growth in its specialty industrial distribution operations over the three-year review period. Revenue has grown at a compound annual growth rate consistent with the broader industrial distribution sector, supported by both organic volume growth and moderate pricing increases passed through to customers in response to input cost inflation.

Revenue is recognized at the point of delivery or shipment, consistent with the requirements of ASC 606, *Revenue from Contracts with Customers*. There have been no material changes in the Company\'s revenue recognition policy during the review period. Revenue is primarily derived from product sales, which constitute approximately 94% of total revenue. The remaining approximately 6% is attributable to ancillary services, including vendor-managed inventory (\"VMI\") programs, kitting services, and custom packaging solutions provided to the Company\'s manufacturing customers. These ancillary services are closely integrated with the Company\'s product distribution operations and are typically provided under multi-year service arrangements that accompany product supply agreements.

**[III.B. Customer Concentration]{.underline}**

The Company\'s top 10 customers represent approximately 31% of 2024E revenue, a level of concentration that is moderate for an industrial distributor and is within the range that Ridgeline considers acceptable for purposes of earnings quality assessment. No single customer accounts for more than 5.5% of the Company\'s total revenue. Customer churn is low; the average customer tenure among the Company\'s top 50 accounts exceeds eight years, and several of the Company\'s largest customer relationships date back more than fifteen years. The consumable nature of the Company\'s product lines --- fasteners, gaskets, and seals that are consumed in customers\' manufacturing processes and require regular replenishment --- provides a high degree of revenue visibility and supports the characterization of HIS\'s revenue as recurring in nature.

**[III.C. Geographic Revenue Distribution]{.underline}**

Revenue is distributed across 14 states, with apportionment factors generally aligned with the Company\'s distribution center locations and the geographic concentration of its manufacturing customer base. The following table summarizes revenue distribution by state based on sales factor analysis:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

The LIFO method has been consistently applied since at least 2001, which is the earliest period available in our S-corporation tax return preparation files. The Company complies with the LIFO conformity requirement of IRC Section 472(c), which mandates that a taxpayer using LIFO for tax purposes must also use LIFO as the primary method for financial reporting. No FIFO or other supplemental inventory valuation disclosures have been made that would violate the conformity requirement.

The Company maintains a LIFO reserve (also referred to as the \"LIFO allowance\" or the \"excess of FIFO over LIFO\") that represents the cumulative difference between inventory valued at current replacement cost under the First-In, First-Out (\"FIFO\") method and the LIFO-basis inventory value reported on the Company\'s balance sheet.

**[VI.C. LIFO Recapture --- Key Consideration for Any Change in Entity Status]{.underline}**

Ridgeline highlights the LIFO reserve of \$11,800,000 as a **key consideration for any change in entity status** or transaction structure involving HIS. Under IRC Section 1363(d), if an S-corporation\'s S-election is terminated --- including by reason of acquisition by an ineligible shareholder, such as a partnership or corporation --- or if the S-corporation otherwise converts to C-corporation status, the **LIFO recapture amount** must be included in the gross income of the S-corporation for its last taxable year as an S-corporation.

The LIFO recapture amount is defined as the excess of the inventory\'s FIFO value over its LIFO value. For HIS, this amount is calculated as follows:

> FIFO Inventory Value: \$76,000,000 Less: LIFO Inventory Value: (\$64,200,000) **LIFO Recapture Amount: \$11,800,000**

This income inclusion creates a **corporate-level tax liability** --- one of the rare circumstances in which an S-corporation incurs entity-level tax. The estimated LIFO recapture tax is as follows:

> Federal corporate income tax: \$11,800,000 × 21% = **\$2,478,000** Michigan corporate income tax: \$11,800,000 × 6% = **\$708,000** Combined estimated LIFO recapture tax (federal and Michigan): approximately **\$3,186,000**

The combined estimate of approximately \$3,186,000 does not include potential additional state income taxes in other jurisdictions where the LIFO recapture income may be apportioned based on the Company\'s multi-state filing footprint. The total state tax exposure could increase modestly depending on the apportionment treatment adopted by each state.

The LIFO recapture tax is payable by the corporation (not by the shareholders individually), and this entity-level tax effectively reduces the net proceeds available to the selling shareholders.

**Important Distinction from Section 1374 Built-In Gains Tax.** The LIFO recapture obligation under Section 1363(d) is separate and distinct from the Section 1374 built-in gains (\"BIG\") tax that can apply to S-corporations that previously operated as C-corporations. The Section 1374 BIG tax imposes a corporate-level tax on recognized built-in gains during a limited recognition period following the S-election. HIS elected S-corporation status effective January 1, 2001, and the five-year recognition period under Section 1374 (as made permanent by the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes Act of 2015, or PATH Act) expired on December 31, 2005 --- nearly twenty years prior to the proposed transaction. Therefore, **Section 1374 built-in gains tax does not apply** to this transaction, notwithstanding that HIS had an estimated net built-in gain of approximately \$14,700,000 at the time of its S-election. The components of that historical built-in gain --- real property appreciation of approximately \$6,200,000, equipment appreciation of approximately \$3,100,000, and LIFO reserve of approximately \$5,400,000 at that time --- are no longer relevant for Section 1374 purposes.

The following is a summary of the key findings from Ridgeline\'s quality of earnings analysis:

1\. **Adjusted EBITDA.** 2024E Adjusted EBITDA of \$41,850,000 is well-supported by the Company\'s financial records. Adjustments totaling \$3,600,000 are rated \"high confidence\" and are comprised of ongoing owner compensation normalization (\$1,800,000) and three genuinely non-recurring items (\$1,800,000 combined).

2\. **Revenue Quality.** Revenue quality is strong, with low customer concentration (no customer exceeding 5.5% of revenue), high customer retention, and recurring demand characteristics inherent in the Company\'s consumable product lines.

3\. **Working Capital.** The Net Working Capital target of \$52,400,000 is appropriate based on trailing twelve-month analysis and is consistent with the Company\'s historical working capital levels.

4\. **LIFO Reserve.** The LIFO reserve of \$11,800,000 represents a significant tax consideration. LIFO recapture tax of approximately \$3,186,000 or more (federal and Michigan combined) will be triggered by any change in entity status, including termination of the S-election upon acquisition by an ineligible shareholder.

5\. **Section 1374 BIG Tax.** The Section 1374 built-in gains tax is **not applicable** to this transaction, as the five-year recognition period expired on December 31, 2005.

6\. **Basis Step-Up.** Aggregate inside tax basis of \$134,200,000 versus enterprise value of \$385,000,000 creates a potential stepped-up basis of \$250,800,000 for the buyer if a stepped-up basis structure is achieved.

7\. **Section 197 Amortization.** Total Section 197 intangible amortization (including goodwill) of \$220,600,000 over 15 years yields an annual federal tax shield of approximately \$3,088,400 for the buyer.

8\. **Inventory Basis Differential.** Inventory at FIFO/FMV (\$76,000,000) exceeds LIFO tax basis (\$64,200,000) by \$11,800,000. This basis differential will provide a near-term COGS tax benefit to the buyer as the stepped-up inventory turns over in the ordinary course of business post-closing.

9\. **Rollover Equity.** David Kressler\'s intended \$12,000,000 rollover equity requires careful tax structuring, particularly in connection with any deemed asset sale election.

10\. **Multi-State Complexity.** The Company\'s multi-state tax footprint across 14 states adds complexity to any structural election and requires state-by-state analysis of conformity with federal tax provisions.
